titleStmt.title: Telegram From the Embassy in Ecuador to the Department of State

div.head: 397. Telegram From the Embassy in Ecuador to the Department of State
div.p: 13627. Subject: Meeting with President Borja, October 25.

2. I met with President Borja on October 25 for an hour’s general conversation, ranging from bilateral questions and adjustment policy to whether Cubans would be involved in his literacy campaign. (They won’t be.) He displayed an impressive grasp of Ecuadorian/Latin American realities, criticizing both Castro and Pinochet. He went on at length to explain his policies and his personal style.

3. I opened by admitting that we did not yet know how the October 24 ICERC debt review had come out (see septel) and I congratulated Borja on the efforts of various ministers in responding to our concerns about his government’s debt policy. I added that I looked forward to dealing with them regarding the adjustment program to assure that the gains made on August 30 would endure. Doing so would facilitate disbursement of the dols 6.5 million under the FY 87 ESF.

4. Responding to my comment that this effort was designed to cooperate rather than to “dictate” any policy to them, Borja explained—somewhat passionately and in considerable detail—that he was an unusually independent person who literally “could not accept” another person or another country telling him what to do. He claimed he had been this way “even with my father when I was four years old.”

5. Following this intense response, we touched the Texaco incident and I urged him to consult with us in advance on such matters in order to avoid frictions. He comfortably acknowledged that the presentation of the decision had been botched by the GOE, and said they had learned
the need for better communications. In any case, He said Texaco had been a good partner and he hoped the company would accept the GOE’s offer of a new “concession”. Comment: An extraordinary word from him, which he subsequently repeated. End comment.

6. We discussed how relations could be improved, and Borja expressed satisfaction that agrement had just been received for Jaime Moncayo as his Ambassador to Washington. I knew of his concern that we believed that 800 Cubans were to be imported for a literacy program. I preempted his denial of that report by explaining that I had traced down the story and had learned that a UNESCO mission on literacy had included two Cubans and two Nicaraguans. Borja thanked me for making this effort, saying that he has begun to see how such rumors were hurting the USG-GOE relationship. He emphatically said that “they’ve already left Ecuador.” He categorically rejected any foreign participation in the upcoming campaign itself. Borja seemed to want to dispel the idea that he was sympathetic to communism. He commented that he tried to be even-handed in his international dealings, “but frankly I don’t enjoy my contacts with Russians—their journalists always ask leading questions and their diplomats try to trap you.”

7. In another vein, Borja said that he had tried to persuade labor unions that the government was defending their interests with his anti-inflation program. “On the other hand, I wouldn’t deceive them” with exaggerated promises, so there will be a national strike (on November 24) “and we’ll hold the line on our policies.” I said that we had reported positively on the GOE’s tight and effective monetary policy; he responded that bank reserve requirements would be hiked again in coming weeks. He bitterly criticized the Febres Cordero government for tolerating massive dishonesty in its exchange-rate regime, and noted that the new rate mechanism resulted in a reduced spread between the trade and free rates (now about 80 sucres, down from over 250 three months ago).

8. Comment: I was surprised by Borja’s knowledge of the details of economic policy and his responsiveness on bilateral matters. This implies both that he is personally involved in the economic programs and that it is not likely to change greatly if there are personnel changes in the cabinet. Also interesting was his explanation of personal style; he approaches the office like a manager, not an autocrat. It was anything but “l’etat c’est moi.” He also said he would try to come to our election-night party, and obviously warmed to a bit of inside gossip on U.S. political developments.

note.p: Source: Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D880953–0506. Confidential; Exdis. Sent for information to Guayaquil.

In telegram 13101 from Quito, October 14, the Embassy sent a lengthy assessment of Borja which began: “Having assumed office with a mandate for evolutionary rather than revolutionary change, Rodrigo Borja has taken a number of positive initiatives during his first two months in office. The economic emergency program announced in late August contains measures needed to begin stabilizing Ecuador’s economy. The tone of internal political discourse—often vitriolic in the past—has been softened, the GOE leadership has listened to divergent opinions, and Borja has demonstrated a commitment to reduce corruption in government and to respect human rights. He has also moved to establish cooperative executive-military relations, to stabilize the labor front, and to support the police in anti-narcotics efforts. At the same time, the new president has had to respond to strong pressures from radicals within his own party and from other extremist elements during his first sixty days.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D880916–0108)

No minutes of this meeting have been found. In telegram 13626 from Quito, October 24, the Embassy reported that Holwill informed Córdova: “about the possibility of an October 24 ICERC decision which could have negative consequences for Ecuador.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D880953–0833)

In telegram 392103 to Bogota, December 5, the Department noted: “The ICERC, a technical committee that passes judgment on foreign bank debt, has informed US banks with exposure in Ecuador that long-term Ecuadorian obligations are ‘value impaired.’ (Banks must set aside reserves against the day they may be forced to write off the loans.)” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D881064–0280) In telegram 15641 from Quito, December 15, the Embassy reported on how Ecuador was adjusting to the value-impaired debt rating. (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D881096–0801)

In telegram 9141 from Quito, September 20, the Embassy reported that on September 19, “Energy Minister Diego Tamiriz announced that the state petroleum firm CEPE would take over from Texaco operation of the Transecuadorian pipeline and of the consortium which produces three-fourths of Ecuador’s crude.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D880840–0715)
